meta.subtitle: 500 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Swedish → English (see the Swedish, recall the meaning) and English → Swedish (see an English meaning, recall the Swedish). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 500 words of Swedish for a beginner, aligned to A1 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand and use familiar everyday expressions and very basic phrases aimed at the satisfaction of needs of a concrete type' — a learner here is able to introduce themselves and others, to ask and answer questions about personal details such as where they live, people they know and things they have, and to interact in a simple way provided the other person talks slowly and clearly and is prepared to help. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: Swedish has examinations at these levels — Swedex and Tisus — but neither was found to publish a word list, so this deck is not an examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 359 of the 500 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — greetings and politeness, introducing yourself, family, numbers, telling the time, days and months, food and drink, shopping and money, the home, the town and getting about, the body and feeling ill, the weather, colours, and the pronouns, question words, prepositions and little words every sentence is built out of — and the other 141 are the commonest remaining words of everyday Swedish, taken from a frequency list built from film and television subtitles and counted by the WHOLE word, every form of a noun or a verb added together. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first. The 165 nouns are printed with their article — en or ett — because the article is the gender, which decides the noun's definite ending, the adjective's ending and the pronoun that stands for it, and they show their definite singular and their plural (bilen, bilar); the 110 verbs show their present, past and supine, the three forms a Swedish verb is learnt by (äter, åt, ätit), and behind the All forms fold their imperative, -s forms and participles. Real example sentences come with 499 of the 500 words, three apiece for 492 of them, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, gender and forms: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: a word list built from OpenSubtitles (hermitdave/FrequencyWords, CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
